Subject: Commit TPS absorption and backstop plan

Tim —

Following up on our sync yesterday: thanks for confirming the intent to move forward with a Dedicated commit. To help procurement and engineering align, I put together an initial approach for mapping your monthly committed tokens to the TPS headroom you’ll need and what our ops backstops look like if you hit bursts. I attached a lightweight model (acme_commit_model.xlsx) — please review.

High-level ask from us: can you confirm the following by EOD Monday so we can finalize the Dedicated sizing proposal?
- Target steady-state committed TPS (tokens/sec) during business hours
- Expected average token length per request (median tokens/request) and typical concurrency pattern (many small requests vs fewer long requests)
- Any firm p95 latency SLO or hard cutoff for tail latency

What we’re proposing (summary):
- Baseline mapping: map committed monthly tokens to an equivalent steady TPS using your daily ramp curve (spreadsheet contains the conversion and a few scenarios).
- Absorption buffer: we recommend a 1.4x GPU capacity buffer vs committed TPS for normal headroom (accounts for model variance, cold KV cache, and short spikes).
- Backstop plan: if the platform detects sustained >1.8x load for >10m, route to a reserved canary pool + fall back to a lower-cost model variant (quantized 8-bit) and enable token-throttling credits for queued work.

Ben & Laura — I’ve put you on this thread for the nuts-and-bolts numbers. Happy to hop on a quick call Wednesday to walk the spreadsheet with Acme engineering.

Thanks,

Thanks Tim — answering inline and adding the compute mapping we used in the spreadsheet.

1) Monthly tokens -> steady TPS conversion- Simple conversion we use in the sheet: steady_TPS = (monthly_tokens) / (30 days * peak_hours_per_day * 3600) * peak_fraction.
- Example: 2.7B monthly tokens, if 10 peak hours/day and peak_fraction 0.6 -> steady TPS ≈ 2.7e9 / (30*10*3600) * 0.6 ≈ 1,500 TPS.

2) Performance and graceful degradation- Our runtime supports continuous batching and an elastic canary pool. For short spikes (<10m) we absorb via prefix cache warmup + ephemeral burst capacity; 95% of requests see slight latency increase (p50 shifts ~10–30%), 5% see tail degradation which we mitigate by routing to a lower-accuracy variant. For sustained overload (>10m) we trigger backstop: reduce per-request max tokens, enable queuing with token-credit consumption, and shift lower-priority routes to hosted fallback.

Compute mapping (from the attached sheet):
- Model variant A (open-xxl-70B q4_k): ~60 tokens/sec per H100-equivalent GPU for 2k-context multi-turns; ~95 tok/s for short context <512 tokens.
- Model variant B (quant-8 70B): ~140 tokens/sec per H100-equivalent GPU (lower quality, good for backstop routing).
- Buffer policy: we recommend 1.4x steady TPS -> GPU slab sizing to account for cold cache and autoscale time. For Acme’s stated 1,200 TPS steady target:
  * Steady capacity need (model A, conservative for mixed context): 1,200 / 60 = 20 GPUs -> apply 1.4x buffer => 28 GPUs reserved
  * Backstop capacity (model B): 1,200 / 140 ≈ 9 GPUs (can be smaller, autoscaled)

Operational notes:
- Warmup: pre-warm KV cache for top 20% of prefixes during known launch windows.
- Quiet-hours scaling: we can run a smaller slab and warm up quickly via pre-warmed kernels and pre-populated KV snapshots.

I’ll update the spreadsheet with the step-by-step math and run three scenarios (conservative / baseline / optimistic) so procurement has numbers to choose from.

Ben Carter
Capacity Planning, Redwood Inference

Sara —

We’ll convert 2.7B/month into three committed token recommendations in the attached spreadsheet: baseline (steady TPS assuming 10 peak hours), buffer (1.4x steady), and peak-friendly (enough tokens to support 1.8x sustained bursts for short windows). I’ve added the SRE checklist paragraph to the draft runbook (slo_backstop_runbook.pdf):

SRE checklist (summary):
- Automation: load monitor triggers at 1.4x and 1.8x thresholds; first-tier automation scales canary slab and reduces per-request max_tokens; second-tier automation enables fallback routing to quantized model variant and activates queued token credits.
- Paging: 1.4x sustained for >15m -> ops on-call notified; 1.8x sustained for >10m -> escalation to capacity engineering.
- Fallbacks: lower-accuracy quantized variant, hosted fallback (limited throughput), and token-credit queueing.

- Laura: draft a one-page SRE blurb for Acme’s internal docs based on the runbook (due Wednesday).
